title: This Year, Make Better Choices with Warren Buffett’s 25-5 List Technique
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart names the professional disease he calls Yes-itis, the habit of saying yes to good opportunities in a way that crowds out great work, and offers Warren Buffett's 25-5 list as the corrective. The procedure is to brainstorm twenty-five goals for the year without editing, then select the five that matter most. The move that gives the piece its force is the third step, which contradicts the obvious reading: the remaining twenty goals are not a secondary list to chip away at but an Avoid Like the Plague list, because those are the good things most likely to distract you from the great ones. He models the exercise with his own goals, from AP World History passing rates to returning essays within two instructional days, and notes that mandatory duties such as grading belong on the list only where there is genuine discretion in how well or fast they are done. The argument rests on his claim that careers are made by hundreds of small choices rather than by one lucky posting. He closes with the observed pattern that aiming at less produces more, and suggests the same holds for students.
points: The twenty discarded goals become an explicit avoidance list, which is the counterintuitive heart of the technique and the step most readers get wrong.
Stuart tells readers to complete the brainstorm and the cut before reading the third step, because knowing the twist in advance corrupts the honesty of the list.

He distinguishes non-negotiable duties from discretionary quality, keeping grading off the goal list while making essay return speed a legitimate target because quick feedback is the only useful feedback.
The framing claim is that professional dreams are realized through deliberate practice and hundreds of small decisions, not through finding the perfect job posting.
For items that cannot be dropped without losing your job, he asks for an efficiency plan decided now rather than improvised later.
quotes: I'm no expert here — just last spring I took on my most recent “This was a poorly considered decision” project — but I do know of one simple, powerful technique for making our yeses much wiser. And before you dismiss the article, let's be clear: a lot is at stake in what we decide to say Yes to.

Some of those are things I've been thinking about for a long time; others just came to me while brainstorming. The only way to get this part “wrong” is to edit yourself during the list-making process.

It's worth saying that, when making my list, I'm not really including things that I need to do as part of my job. For example, grading essays isn't optional for me. However, there is some flexibility in how quickly I get essays back to students; I know quick feedback is the only useful feedback, so increasing my return speed would be a great way for my students and me to grow.
Now that you've got all your hopes and dreams for the year on a single document, go through and pick the five most important ones. Don't treat this task lightly.

Those 20 leftover tasks are now your Avoid Like the Plague list. Seriously: nothing this year will tempt you toward distraction as much as that remaining list of 20 good goals you just brainstormed. Anticipate now how you will avoid pouring more time and effort into those non-top-five goals this school year.

Yet the more I read about success and what it takes to get there — across time periods and disciplines — the more I see a thick, consistent thread: when we decide to aim at less, we end up achieving more. I think our students do, too.
